title: Kumbhara: clay, community and temple service
lead: A cooking pot, a lamp and a ring lining a well answer different needs. Following their makers takes us from everyday household work to a particular temple-service community—and shows why Odisha’s pottery histories need to be told locally.
author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

sections.title: A recorded name, not a founding date

paragraphs.text: A. Stirling’s 1825 account of Orissa Proper or Cuttack lists Kumhar beside Cumbhacara and the occupation “Potter”. The table survives in a later Census of India compilation. It provides a dated written association between a name and a craft, not the moment a community came into existence.

The surrounding caste classifications and ancestry stories cannot be accepted as genealogy. Nor does an old pot identify its maker’s caste. To ask how particular Kumbhara communities formed, we need evidence about families, settlements, work and institutions, alongside the traditions people tell about themselves.
paragraphs.locator: Critical historical scope; no archaeological caste identification

sections.title: Puri: service records and an origin tradition

paragraphs.text: Louise Allison Cort and Purna Chandra Mishra studied the Kumbhara Bishoi between October 1979 and February 1981. This particular hereditary temple-service community supplied Jagannatha’s kitchen from Kumbharapada, Tikarapada and Gopalpur. Their account describes red, faceted cooking vessels for single use; women made small bowls and lamps, while men were inducted into temple service.
paragraphs.locator: Archive introduction; fieldwork scope and division of work

paragraphs.text: The Kurala Purana tells of Vishnu creating the first potter. The researchers describe reading it and honouring craft tools at Kurala Panchami. This is an origin tradition and ritual practice, not a datable account of caste creation.
paragraphs.locator: Archive origin tradition and festival description

paragraphs.text: Separately, they report nineteenth- and twentieth-century induction records in the Madala Panji and colonial land documents. Those records address service and tenure. Their underlying manuscripts were not inspected for this article, and the study does not establish unchanged practice today.
paragraphs.locator: Researchers’ account of documentary records; direct manuscript limit

sections.title: Bhadrak: pots for a whole household

paragraphs.text: A different setting appears in a study by T. Panda and colleagues, published in 2019. Between December 2015 and November 2017, they interviewed 79 experienced artisans across Bhadrak’s seven blocks. Their account describes rural Kumbhara pottery as a livelihood often combined with small-scale farming.
paragraphs.locator: Printed325abstract and327methods; original regional field study

paragraphs.text: The objects went beyond cooking and storage vessels. Portable stoves, lamps, coin-saving kumpi and kua-nanda rings for shallow wells met distinct household needs. Local demand and the availability of clay mattered. These examples show why a potter’s knowledge included matching material and form to a particular use.
paragraphs.locator: Table1 printed328; interpretation of documented repertoire

paragraphs.text: The researchers recorded blackish-grey wares from closed kilns and a preference among buyers for unpainted ritual pots. They also reported competition from plastic and metal and limited returns. Those are findings from the study period, not current prices or a statewide account of every potter family.
paragraphs.locator: Printed329–330; dated craft and economic observations

sections.title: Heritage with its local differences intact

paragraphs.text: Puri’s temple-service history and Bhadrak’s household pottery study answer different questions. Neither makes every potter a temple servant or every vessel part of one ritual. The examples also show why calling a practice traditional requires detail: which place, which object, which occasion and which period?

A fuller community history can connect such records with local family accounts, settlement documents and changing markets. No single founder or deliberate creation of all Kumbhara communities is established here. Preserving the craft’s place in Odia life need not turn an inherited occupation into an obligation for every descendant.
